Gold falls toward $3,800 as Fed hawks reinforce rate-hike outlook
Brent settles higher in choppy trade amid Hormuz attacks, U.S.-Iran tensions
At hearing, US Navy chief blasted over Iran war and its toll on sailors
Gold prices hover near 13-month low in subdued trading
Gold’s worst enemy right now is a 5% Treasury yield, not the headlines from the Middle East
body: A break below $3,800 removes a key psychological level and leaves gold exposed to further selling if the Fed minutes sound hawkish. Gold miners and silver are likely to stay under pressure, though silver has been holding up better in recent sessions. For traders, gold is now trading as a rates instrument: US yields and Fed pricing matter more than geopolitical headlines. A spike in oil prices from the Iran war would likely add to the pressure by lifting inflation expectations and Fed hike bets. Any dovish surprise from the Fed would be the main trigger for a short-covering bounce.
A year ago gold was rallying on hopes of Fed cuts. Today it is under $3,800 because the Fed is hiking, and even the Iran war is working against it.

Gold fell below $3,800 an ounce in Asian trade on Wednesday, extending a slide to its lowest in more than a year as markets brace for a Federal Reserve rate hike next month. Spot gold dropped about 1.4% to around $3,795, after touching a low near $3,792, while futures fell almost 1.8%.

The driver is the same one that has dominated the past week: a Fed that is tightening rather than easing. Markets price roughly a 96% chance of a quarter-point hike in December, according to CME’s FedWatch tool, with a small chance of a half-point move. Fed Governor Christopher Waller added to those bets last week when he said a half-point hike may be needed if core inflation runs hot. US 10-year Treasury yields are hovering around 5.1%, and the dollar is near its strongest level in 19 months.

That combination works against gold on two fronts. Higher yields raise the opportunity cost of holding a metal that pays no income, and a stronger dollar makes it more expensive for buyers using other currencies.

The contrast with a year ago is stark. In November 2025, gold was beginning its climb to a record high as markets expected two or three Fed rate cuts in 2026. Twelve months on, the outlook has flipped from easing to tightening, and gold has given back a large part of those gains.

The Iran war has not provided the support many would expect. Rather than acting as a safe haven, gold has fallen as geopolitical risk has pushed up oil prices, which feeds into inflation, firms up Fed hike expectations and lifts yields. In this cycle, escalation in the Middle East has tended to hurt gold rather than help it.

Banks are adjusting their forecasts. Goldman Sachs analysts Lina Thomas and Daan Struyven have cut their end-2026 target to $4,150 an ounce from $4,650, arguing that a hawkish Fed could block the support gold usually gets from falling yields. Even the lower target implies a recovery of roughly 9% from current levels in a little over six weeks, which shows how quickly the outlook has shifted.

Attention now turns to the minutes of the Fed’s October meeting, due later on Wednesday in the US. A hawkish tone would reinforce December hike expectations and could push gold lower still, with some analysts watching support near $3,708. A softer message, or any sign that the Fed is uneasy about the recent sell-off in technology stocks, could give gold room to recover. For now, the market’s message is clear: as long as the Fed is hiking, gold is struggling to find buyers.

news.title: Morgan Stanley sees USD/JPY fair value above 170, forecasts yen at 162 by late 2027
body: A tier-one bank backing USD/JPY upside at these levels puts it in direct opposition to Japan’s Ministry of Finance, which has been warning about intervention near 160. That makes the pair asymmetric: it could grind higher on rate differentials, but intervention could drop it sharply in a single session. The Fed’s repricing is the main driver, so US data and Fed speakers matter more for USD/JPY than anything from Tokyo short of intervention. The short EUR vs AUD call gets support from today’s Australian wage beat, while the CHF leg leans on the franc’s safe-haven appeal while Middle East risks persist.
Morgan Stanley says a well-flagged December BOJ hike is no match for a Fed that is still tightening, and it is willing to bet against the yen right at Tokyo’s line in the sand.

Morgan Stanley says long USD/JPY remains its preferred trade based on its fair value model, and sees room for further gains as markets reprice the outlook for Federal Reserve rate hikes. The bank has estimated fair value for the pair above 170, well above the current level of around 159.5.

Its case rests on the yen’s sensitivity to global bond yields. Morgan Stanley has described the yen as the G10 currency most exposed to rising yields worldwide, and argues there is limited room for the Bank of Japan to surprise markets with a more hawkish move than is already expected. With US yields climbing on expectations that the Fed will keep tightening, that combination continues to favour the dollar against the yen.

The longer-term view points the same way. Morgan Stanley strategists including Serena Tang forecast the yen weakening to 162 per dollar by the fourth quarter of 2027. They argue that strong global risk appetite, Japan’s terms of trade and the continued appeal of carry trades will outweigh support from narrowing interest rate differentials. Goldman Sachs has taken the opposite view on the yen, a split that shows how hard the currency has become to call.

The bank is also staying short the euro against the Australian dollar and the Swiss franc. The Australian leg looks better supported after stronger than expected wage data on Wednesday added to the case for a hawkish Reserve Bank of Australia.

The main risk to the USD/JPY trade is Tokyo. The pair is trading just below 160, where Japanese officials have stepped up warnings about intervention, and MUFG expects action somewhere between here and 164, this year’s high. The last official intervention drove the pair from around 164 to 155 in under a week, a reminder of how quickly a crowded position can unwind.

The Bank of Japan is widely expected to raise its policy rate from 1.25% in December, and Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Wednesday that the bank will keep tightening. Morgan Stanley’s argument is that a well-flagged hike will not be enough to turn the yen while the Fed is also raising rates. For yen bulls, the turning point would need either a pause from the Fed or a much faster pace of tightening from Tokyo.

news.title: Ueda keeps December hike in play as BOJ wants inflation anchored around 2%
body: Ueda’s remarks reinforce December hike expectations without adding a fresh hawkish trigger, so the yen reaction is likely to be modest. His point that financial conditions remain accommodative supports the view that the BOJ has more tightening to do beyond December, which should keep upward pressure on short-end JGB yields. The rate gap with a Fed on a hiking path still dominates USD/JPY, which is holding near 160 where Tokyo has warned about intervention. Oil remains the wildcard: higher energy costs from the Iran war would push import prices and underlying inflation up, strengthening Ueda’s case.
Ueda gave the market more of the same, more hikes ahead and no panic over the food tax cut, and that is exactly what a central bank heading towards December wants to say.

Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Wednesday that the central bank will keep raising its policy rate in line with economic, price and financial developments, reaffirming the tightening path ahead of next month’s policy meeting.

Ueda said it was important to see inflation anchored around the bank’s 2% target, and noted that financial conditions remain accommodative. That suggests he sees room to lift rates further without choking off growth. His comments follow the bank’s October decision to hold its policy rate at 1.25%, when he declared that underlying inflation had reached 2% and signalled strong prospects for a hike in December.

A large part of his remarks addressed the government’s planned cut to the consumption tax on food. Ueda said the impact of the tax cut was likely to stay limited, but described its effect on the economy and on underlying inflation as highly uncertain for now. He said the bank would assess how the cut feeds through to underlying inflation and set policy accordingly.

The distinction matters for markets. A cut to the food consumption tax would mechanically lower headline inflation when it takes effect, which could make price data look softer than the underlying trend. Ueda’s focus on underlying inflation signals that the Bank of Japan is unlikely to treat a tax-driven drop in prices as a reason to stop raising rates. At the same time, his caution about the uncertainty leaves him room to adjust if the cut boosts spending more than expected.

The comments come after stronger than expected export data earlier on Wednesday, which showed shipments up 20.5% in October and a narrower than forecast trade deficit. Third-quarter GDP contracted slightly, but the bank has pointed to firm wage growth as the stronger signal.

For the yen, Ueda’s remarks reinforce expectations of a December hike without adding a new hawkish signal. With the Federal Reserve also on a hiking path, the rate gap is likely to keep USD/JPY close to the 160 level until the Bank of Japan moves faster or the Fed pauses. Friday’s national inflation data is the next test.

news.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6654 – Reuters estimate
body: The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets.

China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours.

Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations.

Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks.

As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.

In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.
